items.prompt: The retry bug touches Payments, Fulfillment, and Search. Per this unit, what makes it a staff-scope problem rather than a senior-scope one?
choices: It's harder to fix than a normal bug
No single team's roadmap will fix it on its own — it needs judgment applied across teams
It was found by a senior engineer
It involves a vendor API
items.explanation: Scope is about how many teams' decisions your judgment is expected to shape, not difficulty. The retry bug is a senior-scope problem three times over (one per team) and a staff-scope problem once, because closing it for good requires judgment that spans teams no single roadmap owns.
items.reference:
Senior scope

Owns outcomes for their own team

Staff scope

Owns outcomes no single team's roadmap fixes alone

Why: scope is about how many teams' decisions your judgment is expected to shape, not how hard your own team's work is.
items.learnMore:
Scope, not difficulty

Staff scope means being expected to own outcomes across teams that don't report to you, using technical direction and org-level leverage — not personal output, however excellent, bounded to your own team.

items.prompt: This unit's attention framework asks three questions in order before technical direction outranks personal execution. What are they?
choices: Cost, difficulty, and deadline
Blast radius, recurrence, and leverage of a systemic fix
Seniority, team size, and budget
Popularity, visibility, and political risk
items.explanation: The three questions are blast radius (how many teams/how much risk), recurrence (one-time or an ongoing pattern), and systemic-fix leverage (does one fix really transfer to everyone).
items.reference:
QuestionAsks
Blast radiusHow many teams / how much revenue or risk?
RecurrenceOne-time, or a pattern that keeps reappearing?
Systemic-fix leverageDoes one fix really transfer to everyone?
items.learnMore:
Three questions, in order

A problem must score high on blast radius, recurrence, and systemic-fix leverage before technical-direction-plus-sponsorship outranks personal execution — a high score on just one isn't enough.

Nothing; it should still get the technical-direction treatment
items.explanation: The framework explicitly warns that some problems only look systemic. If the causes are actually unrelated, a single shared fix wouldn't transfer — that fails the systemic-fix-leverage question specifically, even with wide blast radius.
items.reference:

items.prompt: Why does the framework require all three questions to score high, not just one, before technical direction outranks personal execution?
choices: Because any single high score is sufficient on its own
Because a problem can be wide-reaching but non-recurring, or recurring but not actually fixable with one shared solution — each question rules out a different false positive
Because the three questions always produce the same answer anyway
Because the framework is only decorative and doesn't actually filter anything
items.explanation: Each question guards against a different way a problem can look bigger than it is: wide but one-off, recurring but not shared-cause, or shared-cause but not actually fixable with one systemic solution. Requiring all three catches false positives a single question would miss.

items.explanation: The framework isn't a ban on writing code — narrow, time-critical, ownerless problems are exactly where the coordination cost of building cross-team consensus would make things slower than just fixing it directly.

🔒 No clear owner: a security patch that can't wait for consensus
